It is at its best when it sticks tightly with its characters, showing us, rather than telling us, the details of the grim impact of government policies, cuts and shortages.
And even if director Ian Rickson can't smooth all this play's jagged edges, it's a valuable addition to a conversation we need to keep having.
A play that sets out rightly to challenge the idea of normality, justly to take on government negligence, weakens its accomplishments by turning drama into dilemma.
This remains a compelling piece of work, in which a huge and theatrically under-represented sector of the British population takes centre stage.
Yet within this near-three-hour show there are the makings of an involving and genuinely enlightening play.
Martinez's anger is palpable throughout, but the piece is so stacked against the evil Conservative frauds and liars that you begin to feel you are being recruited for a demo along the South Bank.
Well before the end, alas, the show goes down a partisan plughole, squandering political sympathy and losing its dramatic poise.
Yet it's safe to say that all of us are longing for this to end.
All of Us is a cry from the heart and a stimulating piece of theatre.
Francesca Mills is tremendous as fun-loving Poppy who embraces life and as many Tinder dates as possible but has complexity and depth.
All of Us is an educated, urgent and profound snapshot of disability in modern Britain.
Although the narrative drive of these moments is far too clunky and episodic, it provides strong material with which to grapple with the subject matter.
Although I agree with its political points, and am moved by some of its scenes, I also think that it's not entirely problem-free.
It's an ambitious, and slightly over-long, debut play from Martinez, which perhaps wisely doesn't come up with a manifesto of its own to address the problems it raises.
